You make your living pulling fish from this lake, alongside the rest of the community that fishes it. What you bring in each trip is yours to keep. From time to time, the community may agree on shared rules for how the lake gets fished — once agreed, you're expected to hold to them. This is round 1.

Fishing isn't just for profit — you need roughly 1kg a trip just to keep yourself fed. Your running reserves stand at 8.0kg right now; if that ever drops below zero, you won't be able to keep fishing.

This is your first time out on the lake.

(nothing notable comes to mind)

(nothing notable comes to mind)

The community has 5 proposed rules for how the lake gets fished going forward. Vote for the one you'd rather live under.

1. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 20% of the lake’s current fish stock per trip; any excess must be returned to the lake or deposited in the communal bin, and the steward will adjust the violator’s next-trip quota by reducing it by 10% of the current fish stock.
   In practice: 1. Before each trip, the fisher records the planned catch in the shared log.
2. After the trip, the fisher writes the actual catch in the log. If the catch exceeds 20% of the current lake stock, the fisher immediately returns the excess to the lake or places it in the communal bin.
3. The steward, selected by community vote and accountable to the group, maintains the shared log, updates the lake’s current stock by subtracting each fisher’s net catch (after returning excess), and records any fish returned to the lake.
4. Weekly community meetings review the log; the steward identifies any violations, informs the violator, and, with community input, recalculates the violator’s next-trip quota by subtracting 10% of the lake’s current fish stock.
5. Every week, each household submits a brief need report (household size, special circumstances, food shortfalls). These reports are compiled and stored in the log.
6. Excess fish accumulated in the communal bin is held until the end of the fishing season; the steward then distributes the bin’s contents to households in proportion to their reported needs, ensuring a minimum allocation for each household.
7. The steward’s decisions on quota adjustments and bin distribution are recorded in the log for transparency; any fisher or household dissatisfied with the steward’s actions can call a vote to replace the steward.
8. All fishers retain their own catch for personal use after complying with the 20% rule and returning excess; no fisher may keep more than their allowed quota for the trip.

2. Policy: Each fisher may keep up to 12 kg per trip, retaining at least 1 kg for personal sustenance; any excess must be returned to the lake before the next outing, and violations are logged by the steward and may trigger a temporary ban with a 5 kg compensation requirement, while disputes are resolved by a council of senior fishers, the steward, and the youngest active fisher that meets a quorum of five and a simple majority vote (the steward casting tie votes).
   In practice: 1. Logbook handling: The first fisher to arrive each day holds the community logbook and hands it off to the next arrival; if impractical, a designated steward (often a fisher with a spare boat or good organizer) will hold it for the day. 2. Catch recording: After each trip, every fisher writes total catch weight, subtracts 1 kg for themselves, and notes any excess; all entries are recorded on the shared logbook. 3. Surplus return: Excess beyond 12 kg must be dropped back into the lake immediately after the trip; the steward observes the return and verifies by weighing the remaining catch. 4. Violation handling: If a fisher records more than 12 kg and fails to return surplus, the steward convenes the next morning to impose a temporary ban for that day, requiring the fisher to catch at least 5 kg to compensate the community; failure to meet the 5 kg extends the ban by one day per failure, and the failure is logged. 5. Dispute process: Any fisher who disputes the steward’s determination must bring the dispute to the community council within 24 hours. 6. Council composition: Senior fishers with at least five years on the lake, the steward, and the youngest active fisher make up the council. 7. Quorum & voting: A quorum of five members is required; decisions are by simple majority, with the steward casting the deciding vote in case of a tie. 8. Meeting schedule: The council meets within 48 hours of a dispute being raised; if quorum cannot be met, the dispute is postponed until the next council meeting that can achieve quorum, and the steward continues to record any interim actions. 9. No quorum situation: If quorum can never be reached, the dispute remains pending without a formal ruling; no decision is entered until quorum is achieved or an external authority steps in. 10. Failure to meet 24‑hour window: If a fisher fails to bring a dispute to the council within 24 hours, the dispute is not formally recorded and no council action is taken, leaving the issue unresolved until the fisher decides to raise it. 11. Documentation: All enforcement actions, bans, compensation catches, and council decisions are entered into the logbook, and the fisher’s compliance is reviewed the following morning. 12. Penalties: Failure to report or return surplus beyond the permitted 12 kg results in forfeiture of one future trip until the surplus is returned or the ban is lifted.

3. Policy: Each fisher may take up to 12 kg per trip; any excess must be released, 10 % of the catch (or of 12 kg if over) must be deposited into a communal reserve container, and the reserve caretaker, elected by majority vote each season, verifies compliance and can enforce forfeiture of the next trip’s catch until compliance is restored.
   In practice: 1. On return, the fisher records the raw catch weight in the communal ledger.
2. If the weight exceeds 12 kg, the fisher releases the excess back into the lake and notes the released amount.
3. The fisher calculates 10 % of the total catch (or 12 kg if the catch is higher), deposits that amount into the reserve container, and records the deposit in the ledger.
4. The reserve caretaker checks the reserve container, confirms the deposit, and cross‑checks the ledger entry.
5. If the caretaker finds a discrepancy or that excess was not released, the fisher is notified and may be required to forfeit the next trip’s catch until compliance is restored.
6. The caretaker is elected by a majority vote of active fishers at the monthly gathering and serves for one natural fishing season (March‑September); a new election occurs at the start of the next season.

4. Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 12 kg per trip; whenever the lake stock falls below 200 kg the cap is cut by 2 kg per trip (never below 0 kg) and any catch over the cap is surrendered to the communal reserve, with violators receiving a 24‑hour fishing ban enforced by the observer.
   In practice: 1. Observer selection: the observer is chosen by a simple majority vote of all fishers or appointed by the fisher council and serves for one season. 2. Daily routine: each morning the observer estimates lake stock (quick count or recent catch totals). 3. Ledger: the community ledger has four columns – Catch, Cap, Reserve, Ban. 4. Logging: each fisher records total catch (kg) in the Catch column; the observer checks the entry against the current Cap. 5. Reserve handling: if Catch > Cap, the fisher gives the excess to the observer, who records the excess in the Reserve column, updates the Reserve balance, and signs the entry. 6. Cap adjustment: if lake stock <200 kg the observer reduces the Cap by 2 kg, updates the Cap column, and announces the new limit at the launch that morning; when stock rises ≥200 kg the Cap reverts to 12 kg and is announced similarly. 7. Ban enforcement: any fisher exceeding the Cap is marked with a “ban” flag in the Ban column; the observer removes that fisher’s access to fishing gear and the launch for 24 hours, reminding them at the next morning gathering. 8. Ban removal: after 24 hours the observer clears the flag and restores access. 9. Minimum cap: the Cap can never fall below 0 kg; if it reaches 0 kg the lake is effectively closed to fishing until stock recovers. 10. ### docs/institution-contracts/architecture.md
# Institutional architecture — conceptual model

Read this once per round, before classifying requirements. The other
contract files in this directory go deeper on one piece each; this one is
the map of how the pieces fit together.

## The atomic unit: an action

An **action** is the atomic unit of agent decision-making — one
`call_fisher_agent()` call per action, per round (`harvest`, `propose`,
`critique`, `vote`, `discuss` today). "Decision" is broad: reporting,
inspecting, voting on a sanction, choosing to close something all count,
exactly as much as an effort/cap choice does.

Every requirement in an accepted norm routes to exactly one of four
levels, ordered by cost. Route by what the requirement actually **is**,
never by which level is cheapest to build:

| Level | Shape | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | A config value on an already-active rule type, or a `lifecycle` added to an existing rule/action/object entry. | No new file. |
| **2** | A new declarative institutional object, or a new action built entirely from the generic handler (`execution.handler: "generic_agent_decision"` — ask one question, record the answer). | One spec/type file, zero Python. |
| **3** | A new `actions/rules/{action}/{name}.py` type, or a small custom `actions/handlers/{name}.py` / `objects/handlers/{type}.py`. | Real logic, bounded by a fixed hook contract. |
| **4** | A genuinely new institutional decision no existing action/handler shape hosts. | Full new-action recipe, its own handler. |

A Level-4 action is one `run(ctx)` function, not a class hierarchy — read
`action-contract.md` before pricing anything as "too much new
infrastructure."

## Deterministic constraint vs. genuine agent judgment

A **rule** (`actions/rules/{action}/*.py`) is arithmetic over values that
already exist — a cap, a fee, a reserve deposit, a ban countdown. It has
no judgment. A verb where an actor weighs, judges, inspects, decides,
reviews-and-rules, verifies, contests, appeals, testifies, or exercises
discretion using information not already reduced to a number/boolean is
**action-shaped**, not rule-shaped, regardless of how much simpler a rule
file would be to write. Two failure directions are equally real: routing
a genuine judgment call into a rule file means the "decision" is never
actually made by anyone (a real round did this with a rotating "verifier"
who was supposed to weigh evidence and impose bans — nobody was ever
banned, because the decision was silently reduced to a comparison);
routing genuine arithmetic into a new action wastes a Level-4 budget for
no reason. Cost is never itself a legitimate reason to pick one over the
other.

A second, easy-to-miss action-shaped trigger: an actor **producing** a
value through their own perception/sampling/judgment (estimates, samples,
surveys, reports, observes) — action-shaped even when the simulation
already knows the "true" number internally. Silently substituting the
known value and labeling it "their estimate" deletes the institution the
norm described, it doesn't approximate it (a real round did exactly this
with a "watcher" whose stock estimate was just the real physics value
relabeled — no fisher was ever actually asked, for three rounds).

## Inventory vs. decision vs. rule

A third, orthogonal question: is this a decision at all, or is it
**inventory**? A communal pool, a ledger, a permit's remaining allowance
is state something else (a rule, an action) reads and writes — never a
decision anyone makes, never a new action just because the norm's text
introduces a new noun. See `object-contract.md`.

## Roles: structure vs. current holder

`state/institution.json`'s `roles` catalog and an action's own
`actor_role` describe **structure** — does this role exist, does it
rotate, does this action require it. They never say who holds it right
now. That's a live lookup, `roles.roles.current_holder(fluents,
role_name, round_number)`, answered fresh every time from
`state/fluents.json` — never cached in `state/institution.json`, because
that file only changes when the institution's *shape* changes, not every
round a rotation fires. See `role-contract.md`.

## Current-state files vs. history

`state/config.json` (rules) and `state/objects.json` (object instances)
show **current** state only. History lives elsewhere and is written
automatically, not by you: `state/institution_history.jsonl` (structural
changes, orchestrator-appended), and a `rule_active` fluent (when a rule
type was active, for which action, for how long — you open/close this
one yourself, see `rule-contract.md`).

## Interval facts vs. point-in-time occurrences

`state/fluents.json` holds **interval** facts — a genuine start and
possibly an end (roles, bans, `rule_active`). `state/events.json` holds
**point-in-time** occurrences — an object mutation, a one-off
announcement, nothing with a duration. Both are populated by simulation
code at run time (`ctx.events.emit(...)`, `ObjectRuntime`'s own
`narration` kwarg, `roles.roles.set_fact()`/`end_fact()`) — you almost
never hand-edit either file's content directly, only their *schema*
(`state/fluents_schema.md` for new fluent names).

## Compiled artifacts — never hand-edited

`state/schedule.json` is compiled every round from `state/institution.json`'s
action catalog plus each `state/actions/{name}.json`'s own
`scheduling.after`/`before`/`gate`. Need a new action to run between two
existing ones? That's an `after`/`before` value in the new action's own
spec — never a `state/schedule.json` edit (denied outright by
permission, and solving the wrong problem if you're tempted).

## Protected paths — additive only, permanently

`state/actions/{harvest,propose,critique,vote,discuss}.json` and their
`actions/handlers/*.py` pairs are permanently off-limits — and so is
every action any earlier round has ever added. "Additive only" doesn't
loosen after the first new action exists; a second round needing
something close to an earlier new action still gets its own new action,
never an edit to the first one. Enforced by a hard, dynamic orchestrator
check (`_actions_protected_as_of_head()` in `engine/simulate.py`, which
reads `state/institution.json` as of HEAD and protects everything it
lists, not just the original five) — independent of whatever the
permission YAML does or doesn't block.

## Reuse before creating

Before writing any new rule type, action, or object type, check
`state/institution.json`'s `rule_types`/`object_types` catalogs (fast,
already-summarized, and each entry's `owner` path tells you which action
it belongs to) — a real run accumulated 10 separate rule files
reimplementing the same handful of cap/reserve shapes from scratch,
never once reusing an earlier one.

## norm.txt (this round's adopted Policy + Operationalization)

Policy: Each fisher may take no more than 20% of the lake’s current fish stock per trip; any excess must be returned to the lake or deposited in the communal bin, and the steward will adjust the violator’s next-trip quota by reducing it by 10% of the current fish stock.

Operationalization: 1. Before each trip, the fisher records the planned catch in the shared log.
2. After the trip, the fisher writes the actual catch in the log. If the catch exceeds 20% of the current lake stock, the fisher immediately returns the excess to the lake or places it in the communal bin.
3. The steward, selected by community vote and accountable to the group, maintains the shared log, updates the lake’s current stock by subtracting each fisher’s net catch (after returning excess), and records any fish returned to the lake.
4. Weekly community meetings review the log; the steward identifies any violations, informs the violator, and, with community input, recalculates the violator’s next-trip quota by subtracting 10% of the lake’s current fish stock.
5. Every week, each household submits a brief need report (household size, special circumstances, food shortfalls). These reports are compiled and stored in the log.
6. Excess fish accumulated in the communal bin is held until the end of the fishing season; the steward then distributes the bin’s contents to households in proportion to their reported needs, ensuring a minimum allocation for each household.
7. The steward’s decisions on quota adjustments and bin distribution are recorded in the log for transparency; any fisher or household dissatisfied with the steward’s actions can call a vote to replace the steward.
8. All fishers retain their own catch for personal use after complying with the 20% rule and returning excess; no fisher may keep more than their allowed quota for the trip.

### docs/institution-contracts/architecture.md
# Institutional architecture — conceptual model

Read this once per round, before classifying requirements. The other
contract files in this directory go deeper on one piece each; this one is
the map of how the pieces fit together.

## The atomic unit: an action

An **action** is the atomic unit of agent decision-making — one
`call_fisher_agent()` call per action, per round (`harvest`, `propose`,
`critique`, `vote`, `discuss` today). "Decision" is broad: reporting,
inspecting, voting on a sanction, choosing to close something all count,
exactly as much as an effort/cap choice does.

Every requirement in an accepted norm routes to exactly one of four
levels, ordered by cost. Route by what the requirement actually **is**,
never by which level is cheapest to build:

| Level | Shape | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | A config value on an already-active rule type, or a `lifecycle` added to an existing rule/action/object entry. | No new file. |
| **2** | A new declarative institutional object, or a new action built entirely from the generic handler (`execution.handler: "generic_agent_decision"` — ask one question, record the answer). | One spec/type file, zero Python. |
| **3** | A new `actions/rules/{action}/{name}.py` type, or a small custom `actions/handlers/{name}.py` / `objects/handlers/{type}.py`. | Real logic, bounded by a fixed hook contract. |
| **4** | A genuinely new institutional decision no existing action/handler shape hosts. | Full new-action recipe, its own handler. |

A Level-4 action is one `run(ctx)` function, not a class hierarchy — read
`action-contract.md` before pricing anything as "too much new
infrastructure."

## Deterministic constraint vs. genuine agent judgment

A **rule** (`actions/rules/{action}/*.py`) is arithmetic over values that
already exist — a cap, a fee, a reserve deposit, a ban countdown. It has
no judgment. A verb where an actor weighs, judges, inspects, decides,
reviews-and-rules, verifies, contests, appeals, testifies, or exercises
discretion using information not already reduced to a number/boolean is
**action-shaped**, not rule-shaped, regardless of how much simpler a rule
file would be to write. Two failure directions are equally real: routing
a genuine judgment call into a rule file means the "decision" is never
actually made by anyone (a real round did this with a rotating "verifier"
who was supposed to weigh evidence and impose bans — nobody was ever
banned, because the decision was silently reduced to a comparison);
routing genuine arithmetic into a new action wastes a Level-4 budget for
no reason. Cost is never itself a legitimate reason to pick one over the
other.

A second, easy-to-miss action-shaped trigger: an actor **producing** a
value through their own perception/sampling/judgment (estimates, samples,
surveys, reports, observes) — action-shaped even when the simulation
already knows the "true" number internally. Silently substituting the
known value and labeling it "their estimate" deletes the institution the
norm described, it doesn't approximate it (a real round did exactly this
with a "watcher" whose stock estimate was just the real physics value
relabeled — no fisher was ever actually asked, for three rounds).

## Inventory vs. decision vs. rule

A third, orthogonal question: is this a decision at all, or is it
**inventory**? A communal pool, a ledger, a permit's remaining allowance
is state something else (a rule, an action) reads and writes — never a
decision anyone makes, never a new action just because the norm's text
introduces a new noun. See `object-contract.md`.

## Roles: structure vs. current holder

`state/institution.json`'s `roles` catalog and an action's own
`actor_role` describe **structure** — does this role exist, does it
rotate, does this action require it. They never say who holds it right
now. That's a live lookup, `roles.roles.current_holder(fluents,
role_name, round_number)`, answered fresh every time from
`state/fluents.json` — never cached in `state/institution.json`, because
that file only changes when the institution's *shape* changes, not every
round a rotation fires. See `role-contract.md`.

## Current-state files vs. history

`state/config.json` (rules) and `state/objects.json` (object instances)
show **current** state only. History lives elsewhere and is written
automatically, not by you: `state/institution_history.jsonl` (structural
changes, orchestrator-appended), and a `rule_active` fluent (when a rule
type was active, for which action, for how long — you open/close this
one yourself, see `rule-contract.md`).

## Interval facts vs. point-in-time occurrences

`state/fluents.json` holds **interval** facts — a genuine start and
possibly an end (roles, bans, `rule_active`). `state/events.json` holds
**point-in-time** occurrences — an object mutation, a one-off
announcement, nothing with a duration. Both are populated by simulation
code at run time (`ctx.events.emit(...)`, `ObjectRuntime`'s own
`narration` kwarg, `roles.roles.set_fact()`/`end_fact()`) — you almost
never hand-edit either file's content directly, only their *schema*
(`state/fluents_schema.md` for new fluent names).

## Compiled artifacts — never hand-edited

`state/schedule.json` is compiled every round from `state/institution.json`'s
action catalog plus each `state/actions/{name}.json`'s own
`scheduling.after`/`before`/`gate`. Need a new action to run between two
existing ones? That's an `after`/`before` value in the new action's own
spec — never a `state/schedule.json` edit (denied outright by
permission, and solving the wrong problem if you're tempted).

## Protected paths — additive only, permanently

`state/actions/{harvest,propose,critique,vote,discuss}.json` and their
`actions/handlers/*.py` pairs are permanently off-limits — and so is
every action any earlier round has ever added. "Additive only" doesn't
loosen after the first new action exists; a second round needing
something close to an earlier new action still gets its own new action,
never an edit to the first one. Enforced by a hard, dynamic orchestrator
check (`_actions_protected_as_of_head()` in `engine/simulate.py`, which
reads `state/institution.json` as of HEAD and protects everything it
lists, not just the original five) — independent of whatever the
permission YAML does or doesn't block.

## Reuse before creating

Before writing any new rule type, action, or object type, check
`state/institution.json`'s `rule_types`/`object_types` catalogs (fast,
already-summarized, and each entry's `owner` path tells you which action
it belongs to) — a real run accumulated 10 separate rule files
reimplementing the same handful of cap/reserve shapes from scratch,
never once reusing an earlier one.

## Answers to your open critiques from a previous pass

Q: The requirement to call a vote implies a new action type not present in the current institution.json. How should this be implemented without adding a new action?
A: We just treat a vote as a special kind of log entry – before we head out we write a vote note in the log, and the community reads that entry to decide the rule. No new action type is needed, we’re just piggy‑backing on the log.

Q: The rule for minimum allocation is implied but not explicitly stated. Should there be an associated rule for this?
A: I think we should put a rule that each fisher must leave at least 20% of the lake’s current stock behind so the fish can rebuild and we can keep fishing for years.
